## Setup

Today we need two packages. If you have never used them, install them once, in the Console:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "janitor"))
```

Then load them at the start of every session:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

`{janitor}` is not part of the tidyverse. We only need one of its functions, `clean_names()`.

## The data

`iris` comes with R: 150 flowers from three species (`Species`), with four measurements each, in cm.

```{r}
glimpse(iris)
```

---

## 1. Rows

### 1.1 A copy of the data

Create an object called `data` and assign the `iris` data set to it.

::: solution

```{r}
data <- iris
```

:::

### 1.2 `filter()`: keep rows

Remove all flowers of the species `setosa` from `data`, and save the result in an object called `data_no_setosa`.

::: solution

```{r}
data_no_setosa <- filter(data, Species != "setosa")
```

:::

Check the result: `setosa` should be gone, and 100 rows should be left.

::: solution

```{r}
unique(data_no_setosa$Species)
nrow(data_no_setosa)
```

:::

### 1.3 The pipe

The **pipe**, `%>%`, reads as "and then". Write the same step with the pipe: take `iris`, and then keep every flower that is not `setosa`. Save the result as `data_no_setosa_pipe`.

::: solution

```{r}
data_no_setosa_pipe <- iris %>%
  filter(Species != "setosa")
```

:::

The pipe is most useful when you chain several steps. The code below also cleans the column names with `clean_names()`, which comes back in 2.2. After cleaning, `Species` is called `species`:

```{r}
data_no_setosa_clean <- iris %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  filter(species != "setosa")

names(data_no_setosa_clean)
```

The result goes into a new object, so `data_no_setosa` keeps the original names for the next steps.

---

## 2. Columns

### 2.1 `select()`: keep or drop columns

Remove the columns `Sepal.Width` and `Sepal.Length` from `data_no_setosa`, and save the result as `data_no_sepal`.

::: {.solution .smaller}

You can do this in three ways. By position, keeping columns 3 to 5:

```{r}
data_no_sepal <- select(data_no_setosa, 3, 4, 5)
```

By position, dropping columns 1 and 2:

```{r}
data_no_sepal <- select(data_no_setosa, -(1:2))
```

By name, dropping the two sepal columns:

```{r}
data_no_sepal <- select(data_no_setosa, -Sepal.Width, -Sepal.Length)
```

:::

::: solution

```{r}
names(data_no_sepal)
```

All three give the same columns here. Selecting by name is safer: if the order of the columns ever changes, selecting by position silently picks other columns.

:::

### 2.2 Rename columns

Rename all columns of `data_no_sepal` so that the names are in lower case, with `_` instead of `.`. Save the result as `data_no_sepal_lc`.

::: solution

With `rename()`, one column at a time, written as `new_name = old_name`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_no_sepal_lc <- rename(data_no_sepal,
                           petal_length = Petal.Length,
                           petal_width = Petal.Width,
                           species = Species)
```

:::

::: solution

With `clean_names()` from `{janitor}`, all at once:

```{r}
data_no_sepal_lc <- clean_names(data_no_sepal)
names(data_no_sepal_lc)
```

:::
